name: Fatima Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the injection moulding machines at Brightform Plastics. We make food tubs and lids, the ones your takeaway soup comes in. Plastic pellets go into a hopper, the machine melts them and squirts them into a mould, and every eleven seconds the mould opens and out drop four tubs. I check them for flash, that's the thin plastic edge where the mould didn't seal, I box them and I swap the colour or the mould when the job changes. Two weeks of nights, two weeks of days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The nights wear me out, I'm forty-three and it's not like at twenty-five. What I like is that I know those six machines like my own kitchen. Machine three always runs hot, machine five sticks on the left side. I don't need anyone telling me. My partner Daniel runs a shift at the supermarket depot, so we pass each other in the hall like ships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now everyone can stop going on about it. Probably say it in the break room, I don't do anything online except the school's parent group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd mean nothing changes, and that suits me. I don't use AI, never have. My daughter Mina uses it for homework and I don't like it, she copies it and thinks she's learned something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as normal. We've got about two months' money saved, I'd like to make it three, but that's the plan anyway, AI or not. Pay off the car loan next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved. Like a test result came back normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mina copies it. Have you argued about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice. I made her write the answer out by hand after, from memory. She rolled her eyes so far I thought they'd stick. Daniel says I'm old-fashioned. I say I'm right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Brightform that worries you anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put pick-and-place arms on two of the machines last year, the arm takes the tubs out and stacks them. That had nothing to do with AI, it's just a robot. So even in the quiet version, the robots keep coming slowly.

S0.say: Good, now everyone can stop going on about it. I'd say that in the break room, because I don't do anything online except the school's parent group.
S0.think: It'd mean nothing changes, and that suits me. I've never used AI and I don't like how Mina copies homework answers from it.
S0.do: Keeps working her rotating shifts at Brightform and tries to grow savings from two months to three. Pays off the car loan next spring as already planned.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a normal test result.
S0.quote: I made her write the answer out by hand after, from memory. She rolled her eyes so far I thought they'd stick.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima doesn't use AI and distrusts it, mostly through watching her daughter's homework. She quietly flags that robots arrive anyway, with the pick-and-place arms already on two machines. She isn't angry at anyone, just glad to be left alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, they'll do what's cheapest, they always have. I'd tell the girls on my shift to keep their heads down and do good work. Not much else to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it gets my machines. The arms on two of them already do half my job. If they get cheaper and smarter, they go on all six, and then they need one person for twelve machines instead of one for six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save, that's what I'd do. Stop the takeaways, get the savings to three or four months. I wouldn't jump at any courses. I'd wait and see who they keep and why, and try to be the one they keep, by being reliable. Never late, never sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. It sits in your stomach on the drive in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't jump at courses. If Brightform offered one, would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was on paid time and they told me straight it keeps my job, yes. If it's 'learn the computer side in your own evenings', no. I've got two kids and nights. When would I do it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides who they keep, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raj, the shift manager. He likes people who don't cause trouble and who turn up. That's me. But Raj doesn't decide budgets, and the people who do have never seen machine three run hot.

S1.say: It's business, they'll do what's cheapest like they always have. I'd tell the girls on my shift to keep their heads down and do good work.
S1.think: I think it gets my machines, because the arms already do half my job on two of them. If they get cheaper and smarter, they'd need one person for twelve machines instead of one for six.
S1.do: Stops takeaways and builds savings towards three or four months. Waits to see who Brightform keeps and aims to be one of them by never being late or sick, only training if it's on paid time.
S1.feel: Worried, with a feeling that sits in her stomach on the drive in.
S1.quote: They need one person for twelve machines instead of one for six.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima's plan for change is to be the most reliable person on the shift, not to learn new skills. She'd train only on paid time with a clear promise, which is practical given her nights and kids. She doesn't blame anyone; to her it's simply business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in government had better have a plan, because I don't. I'd probably share the parent group's posts about it. I wouldn't be marching, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? Brightform goes fully automatic, tubs are the easiest thing in the world. And Daniel's depot too, they've been testing robot pickers there for years. Both of us at once. That's the bit that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut everything that isn't the mortgage, food and the kids. No holiday, cancel the streaming, sell the second car. Ring my sister Aisha, she's a pharmacist, and ask if she could help us for a few months if it came to it. Then I'd look for any job where a person has to be there, cleaning, care, anything, even if it's less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I wouldn't sleep, and on nights I already don't sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is the warning here. Does that give you any time to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the kind of time I'd use well, if I'm honest. I'd spend the first year hoping it's wrong. That's what I'm like. By the time I believe it, it's here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf? He's fifteen.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to worry. He'd know I was lying, he's sharp. He's talked about doing engineering, and I'd be thinking, engineering for what, but I wouldn't say that to him.

S2.say: Somebody in government had better have a plan, because I don't. I'd share the parent group's posts about it, but I wouldn't be marching.
S2.think: Brightform goes fully automatic because tubs are the easiest thing in the world, and Daniel's depot has been testing robot pickers for years. Both of us at once is the bit that frightens me.
S2.do: Cuts everything but the mortgage, food and the kids, cancels streaming and sells the second car. Asks her sister Aisha for possible help and looks for any job that needs a person, even for less money.
S2.feel: Frightened and sleepless, on top of night-shift tiredness.
S2.quote: I'd spend the first year hoping it's wrong. That's what I'm like. By the time I believe it, it's here.
S2.fieldNote: The real fear is both incomes going at once, since Daniel's depot is as exposed as her plant. Fatima is unusually honest that she'd waste the first year in denial. She would protect Yusuf from her doubts about engineering rather than share them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so the schools and the government should be getting kids ready for it. I'd say it at parents' evening more than at work. At work everyone would just make jokes about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is me hoping it's wrong for four of them. I know that about myself. But Daniel's different, he'd make lists and push me, and I'd go along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pay off the car loan and then put that money into savings every month, maybe get to six months by year three. I'd sit down with Yusuf about what he studies, maybe something with people, like nursing, instead of engineering. For me, I'd keep my head down and do the job till they tell me otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, the slow kind. Like a dentist appointment in five years that you can't cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd steer Yusuf away from engineering. What if that's what he loves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then he does it, it's his life. But I'd want him to have a second thing, a backup. My dad told me to get a trade and it worked for twenty years. I don't know what the trade is now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said Daniel would make lists. What would be on his list for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course, definitely. He'd find something like forklift or food safety. I'd say robots drive forklifts now, Daniel, and we'd have the same argument for five years.

S3.say: It's coming, so schools and government should be getting kids ready for it. I'd say that at parents' evening more than at work, where everyone would just joke about robots.
S3.think: Five years is me hoping it's wrong for four of them, and I know that about myself. Daniel would make lists and push me, and I'd go along.
S3.do: Pays off the car loan, then saves that money monthly towards six months by year three. Talks with Yusuf about a backup path like nursing, while keeping her own head down at Brightform until told otherwise.
S3.feel: A slow, steady fear, like a dentist appointment she can't cancel.
S3.quote: My dad told me to get a trade and it worked for twenty years. I don't know what the trade is now.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time helps Fatima's savings but not her mindset; she expects to stay in denial for most of it. Her energy goes into her son's choices rather than her own. She and Daniel have a running argument she half enjoys, even here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough that there's no excuse for anyone not to plan, including me. I'd say it to my sister and to Daniel. Not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years I can live with. Yusuf would be twenty-five, Mina twenty-one, the mortgage would be nearly done. I'd lose the job, sure, but the family wouldn't be in the hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save, mainly. Overpay the mortgage once the car's done. Somewhere around year five or six, when even I can't pretend, I'd let Daniel find me a course, probably something in care or the school kitchen, where you still need someone standing there. And I'd make sure both kids finished their studies before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit tired already just thinking of it. But not frightened like the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'when even I can't pretend'. What would make you stop pretending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the machines on all six. Or Raj looking at the floor when he talks to me. That's how you know, managers stop looking at you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to make the mortgage overpayments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to my mum's every summer, maybe every other year instead. That would hurt, she's not young. But the kids would understand.

S4.say: Ten years is enough that there's no excuse for anyone not to plan, me included. I'd say it to my sister and Daniel, not online.
S4.think: Ten years I can live with: the kids would be grown and the mortgage nearly done. I'd lose the job, but the family wouldn't be in the hole.
S4.do: Overpays the mortgage once the car loan is cleared, visiting her mum every other summer to free money. Lets Daniel find her a course in care or school catering around year five or six, and makes sure both kids finish their studies first.
S4.feel: Uneasy and a bit tired already, but not frightened like in the fast picture.
S4.quote: That's how you know, managers stop looking at you.
S4.fieldNote: Fatima's comfort with ten years comes from the family timeline, not from any plan for herself. She admits she'd only act once she couldn't pretend any more, and she knows exactly what the sign would be. Retraining is something Daniel would arrange for her, not something she'd seek.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Daniel and I both go at the same time and there's no time to hope it's wrong and then fix it. What would help is somebody, the company or the government, telling us plainly what's coming and paying our wages while we learn something new. Not a website, a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the night shifts. Robots don't mind nights. That's the first thing they'll replace, the jobs nobody wants. And in a way I'd be glad to sleep at night again, I just need a wage to go with it.

headlineQuote: Robots don't mind nights. That's the first thing they'll replace, the jobs nobody wants.
portrait: Fatima Tanaka, 43, runs six injection moulding machines making food tubs at Brightform Plastics, rotating between weeks of nights and days. She has never used AI, distrusts it from watching her daughter copy homework, and sees cost-cutting as simply how business works rather than anyone's fault. Her plan in every picture is to save, keep her head down and be the most reliable person on the shift, and she admits she'd spend most of any warning time hoping it was wrong. AGI in two years frightens her most because her partner Daniel's depot job would go at the same time, while ten years feels survivable because the kids would be grown.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because she and Daniel would both lose their jobs at once with no time to hope it's wrong and then fix it.
whatWouldHelp: Someone from the company or government telling them plainly what's coming, in person rather than on a website, and paying wages while they learn something new.
